[249](#249)    type Item = A;
[250](#250)
[251](#251)    #[inline]
[252](#252)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<A> {
[253](#253)        if (self.rev && self.state > self.stop) || (!self.rev && self.state < self.stop) {
[254](#254)            let result = self.state.clone();
[255](#255)            match self.state.checked_add(&self.step) {
[256](#256)                Some(x) => self.state = x,
[257](#257)                None => self.state = self.stop.clone(),
[258](#258)            }
[259](#259)            Some(result)
[260](#260)        } else {
[261](#261)            None
[262](#262)        }
[263](#263)    }

[434](#434)                Foo
[435](#435)            }
[436](#436)        }
[437](#437)

[440](#440)                true
[441](#441)            }
[442](#442)        }
[443](#443)

[446](#446)                None

[448](#448)        }

[469](#469)
[470](#470)        assert!(super::range(0, 5).eq([0, 1, 2, 3, 4].iter().cloned()));
[471](#471)        assert!(super::range(-10, -1).eq([-10, -9, -8, -7, -6, -5, -4, -3, -2].iter().cloned()));
[472](#472)        assert!(super::range(0, 5).rev().eq([4, 3, 2, 1, 0].iter().cloned()));
[473](#473)        assert_eq!(super::range(200, -5).count(), 0);
[474](#474)        assert_eq!(super::range(200, -5).rev().count(), 0);
[475](#475)        assert_eq!(super::range(200, 200).count(), 0);
[476](#476)        assert_eq!(super::range(200, 200).rev().count(), 0);

[496](#496)        assert!(super::range(-10i128, -1).eq([-10, -9, -8, -7, -6, -5, -4, -3, -2].iter().cloned()));
[497](#497)        assert!(super::range(0u128, 5)
[498](#498)            .rev()
[499](#499)            .eq([4, 3, 2, 1, 0].iter().cloned()));
[500](#500)
[501](#501)        assert_eq!(
[502](#502)            super::range(i128::MIN, i128::MIN + 1).size_hint(),
[503](#503)            (1, Some(1))
[504](#504)        );
[505](#505)        assert_eq!(
[506](#506)            super::range(i128::MAX - 1, i128::MAX).size_hint(),
[507](#507)            (1, Some(1))
[508](#508)        );
[509](#509)        assert_eq!(
[510](#510)            super::range(i128::MIN, i128::MAX).size_hint(),
[511](#511)            (usize::MAX, None)
[512](#512)        );
[513](#513)
[514](#514)        assert_eq!(
[515](#515)            super::range(u128::MAX - 1, u128::MAX).size_hint(),
[516](#516)            (1, Some(1))
[517](#517)        );
[518](#518)        assert_eq!(
[519](#519)            super::range(0, usize::MAX as u128).size_hint(),
[520](#520)            (usize::MAX, Some(usize::MAX))
[521](#521)        );
[522](#522)        assert_eq!(
[523](#523)            super::range(0, usize::MAX as u128 + 1).size_hint(),
[524](#524)            (usize::MAX, None)
[525](#525)        );
[526](#526)        assert_eq!(super::range(0, i128::MAX).size_hint(), (usize::MAX, None));

[530](#530)    fn test_range_inclusive() {
[531](#531)        assert!(super::range_inclusive(0, 5).eq([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].iter().cloned()));
[532](#532)        assert!(super::range_inclusive(0, 5)
[533](#533)            .rev()
[534](#534)            .eq([5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0].iter().cloned()));
[535](#535)        assert_eq!(super::range_inclusive(200, -5).count(), 0);
[536](#536)        assert_eq!(super::range_inclusive(200, -5).rev().count(), 0);
[537](#537)        assert!(super::range_inclusive(200, 200).eq(iter::once(200)));
[538](#538)        assert!(super::range_inclusive(200, 200).rev().eq(iter::once(200)));
[539](#539)        assert_eq!(
[540](#540)            super::range_inclusive(isize::MIN, isize::MAX - 1).size_hint(),
[541](#541)            (usize::MAX, Some(usize::MAX))
[542](#542)        );
[543](#543)        assert_eq!(
[544](#544)            super::range_inclusive(isize::MIN, isize::MAX).size_hint(),
[545](#545)            (usize::MAX, None)
[546](#546)        );
[547](#547)    }

[549](#549)    #[test]
[550](#550)    fn test_range_inclusive_128() {
[551](#551)        use core::i128;
[552](#552)
[553](#553)        assert!(super::range_inclusive(0u128, 5).eq([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].iter().cloned()));
[554](#554)        assert!(super::range_inclusive(0u128, 5)
[555](#555)            .rev()
[556](#556)            .eq([5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0].iter().cloned()));
[557](#557)        assert_eq!(super::range_inclusive(200i128, -5).count(), 0);

# RangeStepInclusive in num_iter - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-iter/latest/num_iter/struct.RangeStepInclusive.html

`pub struct RangeStepInclusive<A> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An iterator over the range [start, stop] by `step`. It handles overflow by stopping.

# range in num_iter - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-iter/latest/num_iter/fn.range.html

## Expand description

Returns an iterator over the given range [start, stop) (that is, starting at start (inclusive), and ending at stop (exclusive)).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
let array = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4];
for i in num_iter::range(0, 5) {
    println!("{}", i);
    assert_eq!(i,  array[i]);
}
```

---

# range_from in num_iter - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-iter/latest/num_iter/fn.range_from.html

## Expand description

Return an iterator over the infinite range starting at `start` and continuing forever.

*Note*: Currently, the `Iterator` implementation is not checked for overflow.
If you use a finite-sized integer type and the integer overflows,
it might panic in debug mode or wrap around in release mode.
**This behavior is not guaranteed and may change at any time.**

---

# range_inclusive in num_iter - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-iter/latest/num_iter/fn.range_inclusive.html

# range_step_inclusive in num_iter - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-iter/latest/num_iter/fn.range_step_inclusive.html

```
pub fn range_step_inclusive<A>(
    start: A,
    stop: A,
    step: A,
) ->
```
[RangeStepInclusive](https://docs.rs/struct.RangeStepInclusive.html)<A> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)## Expand description

Return an iterator over the range [start, stop] by `step`. It handles overflow by stopping.

# num_integer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-integer/0.1.46/num_integer/

## Expand description

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Extended](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtendedGcd.html)- Gcd
- Greatest common divisor and Bézout coefficients
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.IterBinomial.html)- Binomial
- An iterator over binomial coefficients.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Average](https://docs.rs/trait.Average.html)
- Provides methods to compute the average of two integers, without overflows.
- [Integer](https://docs.rs/trait.Integer.html)
- [Roots](https://docs.rs/trait.Roots.html)
- Provides methods to compute an integer’s square root, cube root,
and arbitrary `n`th root.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [average_](https://docs.rs/fn.average_ceil.html)- ceil
- Returns the ceiling value of the average of `x`and`y`– see[Average::average_ceil](https://docs.rs/trait.Average.html#tymethod.average_ceil).
- [average_](https://docs.rs/fn.average_floor.html)- floor
- Returns the floor value of the average of `x`and`y`– see[Average::average_floor](https://docs.rs/trait.Average.html#tymethod.average_floor).
- [binomial](https://docs.rs/fn.binomial.html)
- Calculate the binomial coefficient.
- [cbrt](https://docs.rs/fn.cbrt.html)
- Returns the truncated principal cube root of an integer –
see [Roots::cbrt](https://docs.rs/trait.Roots.html#method.cbrt).
- [div_](https://docs.rs/fn.div_ceil.html)- ceil
- Ceiled integer division
- [div_](https://docs.rs/fn.div_floor.html)- floor
- Floored integer division
- [div_](https://docs.rs/fn.div_mod_floor.html)- mod_ - floor
- Simultaneous floored integer division and modulus
- [div_rem](https://docs.rs/fn.div_rem.html)
- Simultaneous integer division and modulus
- [gcd](https://docs.rs/fn.gcd.html)
- Calculates the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) of the number and `other`. The result is always non-negative.
- [gcd_lcm](https://docs.rs/fn.gcd_lcm.html)
- Calculates the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) and
Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of the number and `other`.
- [lcm](https://docs.rs/fn.lcm.html)
- Calculates the Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) of the number and `other`.
- [mod_](https://docs.rs/fn.mod_floor.html)- floor
- Floored integer modulus
- [multinomial](https://docs.rs/fn.multinomial.html)
- Calculate the multinomial coefficient.
- [nth_](https://docs.rs/fn.nth_root.html)- root
- Returns the truncated principal `n`th root of an integer – see[Roots::nth_root](https://docs.rs/trait.Roots.html#tymethod.nth_root).
- [sqrt](https://docs.rs/fn.sqrt.html)
- Returns the truncated principal square root of an integer –
see [Roots::sqrt](https://docs.rs/trait.Roots.html#method.sqrt).

# num-integer 0.1.44 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-integer/0.1.44

# num-integer

`Integer` trait and functions for Rust.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.1"
```
and this to your crate root:

```
extern crate num_integer;
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature.  Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.1.36"
 = false
```
There is no functional difference with and without `std` at this time, but
there may be in the future.

Implementations for `i128` and `u128` are only available with Rust 1.26 and
later.  The build script automatically detects this, but you can make it
mandatory by enabling the `i128` crate feature.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-integer` crate is tested for rustc 1.8 and greater.

## License

Licensed under either of

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Num](https://docs.rs/trait.Num.html)
- The base trait for numeric types, covering `0`and`1`values, comparisons, basic numeric operations, and string conversion.
- [NumAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.NumAssign.html)
- The trait for `Num`types which also implement assignment operators.
- [NumAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.NumAssignOps.html)- Ops
- Generic trait for types implementing numeric assignment operators (like `+=`).
- [NumAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.NumAssignRef.html)- Ref
- The trait for `NumAssign`types which also implement assignment operations taking the second operand by reference.
- [NumOps](https://docs.rs/trait.NumOps.html)
- Generic trait for types implementing basic numeric operations
- [NumRef](https://docs.rs/trait.NumRef.html)
- The trait for `Num`types which also implement numeric operations taking the second operand by reference.
- [RefNum](https://docs.rs/trait.RefNum.html)
- The trait for `Num`references which implement numeric operations, taking the second operand either by value or by reference.

# num-traits 0.2.19 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-traits/0.2.19/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# libm 0.2.16 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/libm/^0.2.0

`libm`

A Rust implementations of the C math library.

## Usage

`libm` provides fallback implementations for Rust's [float math functions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f32.html) in
`core`, and the [ core_float_math](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/137578) feature. If what is available suits your
needs, there is no need to add

`libm` as a dependency.If more functionality is needed, this crate can also be used directly:

```
[]
 = "0.2.11"
```
## Contributing

Please check [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://docs.rs/CONTRIBUTING.md)

## Minimum Rust version policy

This crate supports rustc 1.63 and newer.

## License

Usage is under the MIT license, available at
[https://opensource.org/license/mit](https://opensource.org/license/mit).

### Contribution

Contributions are licensed under both the MIT license and the Apache License,
Version 2.0, available at [https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0). Unless
you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for
inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be
dual licensed as mentioned, without any additional terms or conditions.

See [LICENSE.txt](https://docs.rs/LICENSE.txt) for full details.

# num-traits 0.2.17 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-traits/0.2.17

# num-traits

Numeric traits for generic mathematics in Rust.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature. Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
 = false
# features = ["libm"]    # <--- Uncomment if you wish to use `Float` and `Real` without `std`
```
The `Float` and `Real` traits are only available when either `std` or `libm` is enabled.

The `FloatCore` trait is always available.  `MulAdd` and `MulAddAssign` for `f32`
and `f64` also require `std` or `libm`, as do implementations of signed and floating-
point exponents in `Pow`.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-traits` crate is tested for rustc 1.31 and greater.

## License

Licensed under either of

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# num-traits 0.2.15 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-traits/0.2.15

# num-traits

Numeric traits for generic mathematics in Rust.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature. Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
 = false
# features = ["libm"]    # <--- Uncomment if you wish to use `Float` and `Real` without `std`
```
The `Float` and `Real` traits are only available when either `std` or `libm` is enabled.

The `libm` feature is only available with Rust 1.31 and later ([see PR #99](https://github.com/rust-num/num-traits/pull/99)).

The `FloatCore` trait is always available.  `MulAdd` and `MulAddAssign` for `f32`
and `f64` also require `std` or `libm`, as do implementations of signed and floating-
point exponents in `Pow`.

Implementations for `i128` and `u128` are only available with Rust 1.26 and
later.  The build script automatically detects this, but you can make it
mandatory by enabling the `i128` crate feature.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-traits` crate is tested for rustc 1.8 and greater.

and `f64` also require `std`, as do implementations of signed and floating-
point exponents in `Pow`.

Implementations for `i128` and `u128` are only available when `i128` is enabled.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-traits` crate is tested for rustc 1.8 and greater.

---

# num-traits 0.2.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-traits/0.2.2

# num-traits

Numeric traits for generic mathematics in Rust.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
and this to your crate root:

```
extern crate num_traits;
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature.  Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
 = false
```
The `Float` and `Real` traits are only available when `std` is enabled. The
`FloatCore` trait is always available.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-traits` crate is tested for rustc 1.8 and greater.

---

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Num](https://docs.rs/trait.Num.html)
- The base trait for numeric types, covering `0`and`1`values, comparisons, basic numeric operations, and string conversion.
- [NumAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.NumAssign.html)
- The trait for `Num`types which also implement assignment operators.
- [NumAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.NumAssignOps.html)- Ops
- Generic trait for types implementing numeric assignment operators (like `+=`).
- [NumAssign](https://docs.rs/trait.NumAssignRef.html)- Ref
- The trait for `NumAssign`types which also implement assignment operations taking the second operand by reference.
- [NumOps](https://docs.rs/trait.NumOps.html)
- Generic trait for types implementing basic numeric operations
- [NumRef](https://docs.rs/trait.NumRef.html)
- The trait for `Num`types which also implement numeric operations taking the second operand by reference.
- [RefNum](https://docs.rs/trait.RefNum.html)
- The trait for `Num`references which implement numeric operations, taking the second operand either by value or by reference.

# num_iter - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-iter/0.1.44/i686-pc-windows-msvc/num_iter/

## Expand description

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- An iterator over the range [start, stop)
- An iterator over the infinite range starting at`start`
- An iterator over the range [start, stop]
- An iterator over the range [start, stop) by`step`. It handles overflow by stopping.
- An iterator over the infinite range starting at`start`by`step`
- An iterator over the range [start, stop] by`step`. It handles overflow by stopping.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- Returns an iterator over the given range [start, stop) (that is, starting at start (inclusive), and ending at stop (exclusive)).
- Return an iterator over the infinite range starting at`start`and continuing forever.
- Return an iterator over the range [start, stop]
- Return an iterator over the range [start, stop) by`step`. It handles overflow by stopping.
- Return an iterator over the infinite range starting at`start`and continuing forever by`step`.
- Return an iterator over the range [start, stop] by`step`. It handles overflow by stopping.
